title: Surrealism: Dalí and Magritte
subject: art
description: Born in 1924, Surrealism set out to free the unconscious: dreams, desires, wild associations. **Dalí** raves, **Magritte** puzzles.

hero.hook: What if reason were a prison, and dreaming the only way out?

blocks.text: **Surrealism** (1924-1969) was not only a style; it was a revolution in thought. After World War I, it set out to fuse dream and waking mind, at the point where the real and the imaginary stop fighting each other.
With **Salvador Dalí** and **René Magritte**, the movement invented a visual grammar the whole world would recognize. One dived into personal delirium, the other into cold philosophical riddles.

The poet **André Breton** founded the movement with the *Manifesto of Surrealism* in **1924**. After [[Dadaism]], which had destroyed meaning, Breton wanted to rebuild the mind by setting thought free. He called it “pure psychic automatism”: writing or painting with no control from reason.

blocks.caption: The 1924 Manifesto: Surrealism becomes a program

blocks.text: Breton collected “primitive” art and curiosities. At his death, his studio held over 5,000 pieces meant to feed the imagination.

The inspiration came from [[Freudian psychoanalysis as a source]]: Sigmund Freud had shown that the unconscious rules the psyche. To slip past inner censorship, the Surrealists invented [[Automatic writing]] and the [[Exquisite Corpse]], the game where each player adds a sentence or a drawing without seeing the one before. The goal was to paint the unreal with a realism so exact that the solid world itself begins to look doubtful.

The Catalan **Salvador Dalí** (1904-1989) joined the group in **1929**. He invented the “paranoiac-critical” method: a deliberate delirium in which he yoked unrelated things together. His phobias became universal symbols.

blocks.caption: The Persistence of Memory: time melting

blocks.text: Dalí had been terrified of grasshoppers since childhood. In his paintings they stand for the fear of passing time and of death.

*The Persistence of Memory* (**1931**) shows soft watches in a landscape drawn from [[Port Lligat]], on the Catalan coast. Breton nicknamed him “Avida Dollars” and expelled him in **1939**. By then Dalí had already turned Surrealism into a worldwide phenomenon, carried by a technique worthy of the Renaissance.

sections.title: Magritte: the mystery of the everyday

blocks.text: The Belgian **René Magritte** (1898-1967) led an ordinary life and often painted in his dining room. His Surrealism is not dreamlike; it is intellectual. He uncovers the mystery hidden inside daily life through visual paradox.

blocks.caption: “This is not a pipe”: the image is not the thing

blocks.text: *The Treachery of Images* (**1929**) writes under a perfectly painted pipe: “This is not a pipe.” The image is a sign, not the object. Bowler hat, apple, clouds: Magritte builds riddles. People sometimes call this [[Magical realism]]: the strange grows out of a familiar world knocked slightly out of true.
Before he could live off his painting, Magritte designed wallpaper and ads for Belgian fashion houses, which explains his taste for repetition and order.
Surrealism runs through film, fashion, and our whole visual culture. After **1924**, art was no longer obliged to copy the outside world: it could dive into the darkest private corners.

events.detail: Two paths: controlled delirium and philosophical riddle.

events.title: The Persistence of Memory
events.detail: The soft watches became a global icon.

blocks.text: Dalí pushed self-expression all the way to extravagance. Magritte questioned the truth of images and pointed toward conceptual art. The movement formally ended with Breton's death in **1966**, but the legacy stayed.
Surrealism freed the unconscious from the control of reason. Dalí invented the paranoiac-critical method; Magritte turned the everyday image into a philosophical riddle.
